Theme 1

Who is the dengue mosquito?

Hi! I'm Duda, a junior agent against dengue. My job is to investigate where the mosquito hides and teach everyone how to keep it from being born. To start, we need to get to know the enemy: Aedes aegypti.

Aedes aegypti is a small, dark mosquito with white stripes on its legs. It lives close to people, inside and around houses, and bites mostly during the day. Only the female bites, because she needs blood for her eggs to develop (ESPÍRITO SANTO, [20--]).

Why talk about dengue?

  • Where? The mosquito lives close to people: around houses, schools and squares, wherever there is standing water.

  • When? With rain and heat, containers fill with water and the eggs turn into mosquitoes faster. That's why cases go up in summer.

  • How do we win? Without standing water, the mosquito isn't born. Just 10 minutes a week checking your home, with an adult, is enough.

On this journey, you'll go from the mosquito to the city: meet the enemy, find out where it is born, protect your home and school, learn to take care of your health and see that dengue is beaten all together.

Portrait of the mosquito

Tap the 7 numbers to learn about each part of Aedes aegypti. Then answer 2 questions to win the star.

Now it's your turn, detective! There are lots of insects flying around the room. Can you find the dengue mosquitoes just by the way they look?

Find the mosquito! 🦟

Find the 4 dengue mosquitoes. The clue: a dark body and white stripes on the legs. Make no more than 3 mistakes to win the star.

A question many people ask: does every mosquito transmit dengue? No! Only a female Aedes mosquito carrying the virus transmits it. She picks up the virus when she bites a sick person.

Does every mosquito transmit dengue?

There are 7 cards. Take each one to the right box: can transmit, not yet, but could start to transmit or doesn't transmit dengue.

Aedes aegypti can transmit three different diseases: dengue, Zika and chikungunya. They are all caused by viruses. Each one has its own signs, but prevention is the same!

Dengue, Zika and chikungunya

Take each card to the right disease. If the information applies to all three, use the All three box. Make no more than 2 mistakes to win the star.

Did you know?

The name Aedes aegypti comes from Greek and Latin and means something like “the unpleasant one from Egypt”, because the mosquito was described from specimens from Africa. Today it lives in almost every warm region of the planet.

In Brazil, Fiocruz and the Ministry of Health release mosquitoes carrying the bacterium Wolbachia, which stops the virus from developing inside the mosquito. It's one more tool, but it doesn't replace getting rid of breeding sites (WOLBITO DO BRASIL, [2025]).

This issue's question

How can each of us help beat dengue? First clue: get to know the mosquito and know that it transmits three diseases.

Theme 2

From egg to mosquito

The mosquito isn't born fully grown! It goes through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult mosquito. The first three happen in water. If we take away the water, the cycle stops!

With heat and water, an egg takes seven to ten days to become an adult mosquito. That's why breeding sites should be eliminated at least once a week (FIOCRUZ, [20--]a).

The mosquito's life cycle

Part 1: tap the stages in the right order to build the cycle. Part 2: move through the days on the calendar and watch the mosquito grow in the water.

The female mosquito is very clever: she lays her eggs on the inside wall of containers, just a little above the water. When the water rises, the eggs get wet and the larvae hatch.

Where does the mosquito lay its eggs?

Part 1: the female mosquito is looking for a place for her eggs. Tap each of the 10 places in the garden, look through the magnifying glass and say: she lays eggs here or not here? Part 2: do the bucket experiment and find out what happens to the eggs when it rains. Get 8 out of 10 right to win the star.

Standing water: that's where danger lives! And it doesn't take much water. A bottle cap, an eggshell or a plant leaf is enough for the mosquito to breed.

It rained in the backyard!

There are 14 objects in the backyard. 1) Before the rain, make your prediction: tap the places that will collect water. 2) Tap Make it rain and check. 3) Fix each breeding site that appeared. Get at least 11 guesses right and fix them all to win the star.

Have you noticed that dengue goes up in summer? That's because rain + heat + standing water is the mosquito's favorite combination. Rain fills the containers and heat makes the cycle faster.

Rain + heat + standing water

Choose the season and how well the neighborhood takes care of standing water. Then see how many mosquitoes are born in 4 weeks. Complete the 3 missions to win the star.

Illustrative numbers, to compare the situations.

Did you know?

Aedes aegypti eggs are very tough: they can survive up to 450 days in a dry place and hatch when they come into contact with water (FIOCRUZ, [20--]b). That's why emptying the container isn't enough: you have to scrub the walls with a sponge or brush.

A single female can lay up to 500 eggs in her lifetime, which lasts 30 to 45 days. And in hot weather, the mosquito reproduces faster (ESPÍRITO SANTO, [20--]).

This issue's question

How can each of us help beat dengue? Second clue: get rid of standing water every week, because without water the mosquito can't complete its cycle.

Theme 3

Breeding site hunt!

A breeding site is any place that collects standing water, where the mosquito can be born. Most of them are inside and around houses: plant pots, tires, bottles, gutters, drains, water tanks and much more. Shall we go hunting?

Breeding site hunt!

This time the hunt is on the roof terrace of the house. There are 10 breeding sites: tap each one and choose the right way to get rid of it. Make no more than 3 mistakes to win the star.

Did you know that 10 minutes a week is enough to keep your home free of breeding sites? This idea was created by researchers at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute, part of Fiocruz. The secret is having a routine (LARA NETO, 2016).

10 minutes against dengue

The house is shown open, like a dollhouse. Take Duda to the 8 places, in any order you like, and choose what to check in each one. Each check takes 1 minute, going in or out of the house takes 1 more minute and a wrong answer costs 30 seconds. Finish in 10 minutes or less to win the star.

Now it's real life! Call an adult from your family and check your home together. Note: don't climb onto roofs, ladders or high places. That's a job for the adult.

Is my home protected?

Answer each checklist item with your family. At the end, you'll see the points to watch and can print the list to stick on the fridge.

Some breeding sites are well hidden: behind furniture, among the plants, under tarps. Today the backyard is dark. Grab the flashlight and let's investigate!

Dengue detectives 🔎

It's nighttime in the backyard. Move the flashlight (drag your finger or the mouse) and tap the 8 breeding sites on the detective's list. A glow appears when the light gets close. Careful: the battery doesn't last long, and not everything in the dark is a breeding site! Find all 8 to win the star.

Taking care isn't a one-time thing! Look at the same recreation area one week apart. What got better? What got worse? Compare the before and the after.

Before and after: keep the backyard protected

The same recreation area, one week apart. Compare the two scenes, tap the 10 differences and say whether each one got better or got worse. Then fix what got worse. Make no more than 2 mistakes to win the star.

Detectives can do math too! Let's count breeding sites, add, subtract, multiply and even read a chart to find out how many are still left to get rid of.

Shall we count the breeding sites?

There are 7 math challenges: count, add, subtract, multiply and read a chart. When you can, tap the drawings to count. Get 6 right to win the star.

Help! There's a plant-pot saucer full of water at the back of the backyard. Help Duda get the bag of sand and reach the pot before the mosquito lays its eggs!

Maze against dengue

Use the arrows (on the screen or the keyboard) or swipe your finger. First get the sand, then reach the pot.

Did you know?

The “10 minutes” idea is simple: since the mosquito takes seven to ten days to be born, one check a week breaks the cycle before the adult leaves the water (LARA NETO, 2016; FIOCRUZ, [20--]a).

To get rid of a breeding site, you can: empty and scrub it, turn it upside down, cover it tightly, store it under a roof, fill it with sand or throw it away the right way.

This issue's question

How can each of us help beat dengue? Third clue: do the 10-minute check at home, every week, with the family.

Theme 4

From school to the city

Schools can have breeding sites too: in the schoolyard, the garden, the sports court, the bathrooms, the storeroom. How about doing an investigation with your class and your teacher?

What about the school, is it protected?

Visit the school's 5 areas and find the 10 problems. For each one, choose what the school should do. At the end, the class gets a report to hand to the principal. Make no more than 3 mistakes to win the star.

Dengue is also a city problem. Waste collection, street cleaning, running water every day and treated sewage help reduce breeding sites. When there's no running water, for example, people store water in buckets and drums, and these need to be tightly covered.

Dengue is also a city problem

Tap the 7 problems on the street. First choose the public service that solves each one. Then say how residents can help. Make no more than 3 mistakes to win the star.

A bottle dumped on a vacant lot, a disposable cup on the sidewalk, an old tire in the backyard… Waste in the wrong place can become a breeding site when it rains! Every kind of waste has a right destination.

Waste in the wrong place can become a breeding site

The rain is coming! Take each piece of waste to the right destination before the cloud arrives. Make no more than 2 mistakes to win the star.

Did you know?

Brazil's basic sanitation law includes four services: water supply, sewage, urban cleaning and solid waste management, and rainwater drainage (BRASIL, 2007). They all help prevent dengue.

The National Solid Waste Policy (Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) says that responsibility for waste is shared: government, businesses and every citizen each have their part (BRASIL, 2010).

This issue's question

How can each of us help beat dengue? Fourth clue: investigate the school and take care of the neighborhood, sorting waste and demanding public services.

Theme 5

Dengue and health

Dengue doesn't pass from one person to another through hugs, coughs or sharing a cup. The mosquito is what carries the virus. Let's see how that happens?

How does the mosquito transmit dengue?

Tap the 6 scenes in the right order to build the story of transmission. Make no more than 3 mistakes to win the star.

How can you tell if it might be dengue? The body gives signs. Knowing these signs helps you tell an adult quickly and get care at the health center.

What are the symptoms of dengue?

Tap the 6 parts of Téo's body to learn about the symptoms. Then find out which are the warning signs that call for urgent care.

Educational content. If you have symptoms, go to a health center.

Is there treatment for dengue? There's no medicine that kills the virus, but there is care: drinking plenty of fluids, resting and following the health team's advice. And no taking medicine on your own!

Taking care of dengue the right way

Follow Téo, who has a fever, and choose the best action at each moment. Get 5 out of 6 right to win the star.

Text based on Brasil ([2026a]; 2024).

Why shouldn't we take medicine on our own? Because each body and each disease needs different care. With dengue, some common medicines can increase the risk of bleeding. Only the health team can prescribe medicine, and an adult is the one who gives medicine to a child.

Do you know who inspires me? The endemic disease control agent! They visit homes, look for breeding sites, advise families and help monitor diseases. It's a profession guaranteed by law (BRASIL, 2006).

The endemic disease control agent

Part 1: put together the agent's kit. Choose the 6 work items (careful: 4 things don't belong!). Part 2: follow the visit and help Lia's family welcome the agent the right way. Get 3 out of 4 right to win the star.

A lot of wrong information about dengue goes around. Before believing it and passing it on, it's good to check it with trustworthy health sources. Shall we test it?

Dengue myths and facts

There are 10 cards, each with a drawing and a sentence. Tap Fact or Myth (or drag the card to the side). Get 8 right to win the star.

Did you know?

Since 2024, Brazil's public health system (SUS) has offered a dengue vaccine. It is offered to some age ranges and groups, which may change over time. Ask at the health center whether you can get it. The vaccine helps a lot, but it doesn't replace taking care of standing water (BRASIL, [2026a]).

People who have had dengue can get it again, because there are four types of dengue virus (BRASIL, 2024).

This issue's question

How can each of us help beat dengue? Fifth clue: know the signs, go to the health center, don't take medicine on your own and welcome the agent.

Axis 6

Everyone against dengue!

Nobody beats dengue alone. Prevention depends on the family, the school, the community and the government. Everyone has a part, and every part matters!

Everyone does their part

There are 8 actions. Take each one to whoever is mainly responsible for it. Make no more than 2 mistakes to win the star.

This issue's question: the answer

How can each of us help beat dengue?

  • Know the mosquito and the diseases it transmits.
  • Don't leave standing water: the mosquito is born in water.
  • Do the 10-minute check at home, every week.
  • Investigate the school and take care of waste and the neighborhood.
  • Know the signs of the disease, go to the health center and don't take medicine on your own.

Together, family, school, community and government, we beat dengue. Everyone against dengue!

      Credits

      About the project

      The Outreach Project Urban and Environmental Literacy (Alfabetismo e Letramento Urbano e Ambiental) is an initiative of the Graduate Program in Architecture and Urbanism at UNIVAG (PPGAU-UNIVAG), carried out in partnership with ANAP – Associação Amigos da Natureza da Alta Paulista and linked to the Research Group City, Society and Landscape (Cidade, Sociedade e Paisagem).

      The project aims to bring the university, schools and society closer together, spreading and popularizing scientific knowledge about cities, the environment, landscape and sustainability in language that children can understand.

      Basic urban and environmental literacy refers to a child's ability to know, recognize and understand the basic elements, concepts and processes related to the city and the environment. It is building the repertoire a child needs to be able to “read” the place where they live.

      Urban and environmental literacy in practice is the next step: it refers to the ability to use this knowledge to interpret, connect, question and take a stand on real situations in their area, and even to propose solutions and take part in actions that bring change.

      One of the project's products is ECO LEGAL Interactive, a digital educational publication whose issues turn knowledge and findings from undergraduate research, master's dissertations, faculty research and postdoctoral studies into interactive content for children.

      Each issue covers a specific theme, combining scientific knowledge, educational language, visuals, games and activities to help develop urban and environmental literacy.

      Issue summary

      Theme

      The issue deals with the Aedes aegypti mosquito and preventing dengue, Zika and chikungunya, based on the central question “How can each of us help beat dengue?”. The content is organized into six themes: “Who is the dengue mosquito?” (recognizing the mosquito, the difference between mosquitoes that do and don't transmit dengue, and the three diseases); “From egg to mosquito” (the life cycle, egg-laying sites, standing water and the relationship between rain, heat and mosquito reproduction); “Breeding site hunt!” (household breeding sites, the weekly 10-minute check, the home checklist, the search for hidden breeding sites, and math and spatial orientation activities); “From school to the city” (investigating the school, public sanitation and urban cleaning services, and the correct disposal of solid waste); “Dengue and health” (transmission, symptoms and warning signs, care without self-medication, the endemic disease control agent, and myths and facts); and “Everyone against dengue!” (the responsibilities of the family, the school, the community and the government). The main 2030 Agenda goal is SDG 3, Good Health and Well-being, connected to SDGs 6, 11 and 12.

      Objective

      To lead children to recognize Aedes aegypti and its life cycle, understand that the mosquito breeds in standing water, identify and get rid of breeding sites at home, at school and in the neighborhood, relate prevention to sanitation and solid waste management, and recognize the signs of the disease and the importance of going to a health service without self-medicating, seeing prevention as a shared responsibility.

      Specific objectives

      • Recognize the features of Aedes aegypti and tell it apart from other insects, such as the common house mosquito.
      • Identify the diseases transmitted by the mosquito (dengue, Zika and chikungunya) and understand how transmission happens.
      • Describe the mosquito's life cycle (egg, larva, pupa and adult) and relate it to the need for a weekly check.
      • Identify breeding sites, including small and hidden ones, and the right actions to get rid of them.
      • Relate rain, heat and standing water to the increase in the number of mosquitoes.
      • Relate prevention to sanitation services, urban cleaning and the correct disposal of solid waste.
      • Recognize the symptoms and warning signs of dengue, the importance of hydration and follow-up by the health service, and the risks of self-medication.
      • Learn about the work of the endemic disease control agent and the role of the family, the school, the community and the government.

      Methodology

      The issue uses game-based learning, in three moments that repeat in every section: the mascot, Duda, a junior agent against dengue inspired by the endemic disease control agent, introduces the topic in a short speech with the key words highlighted; the child plays, investigates and makes decisions; and each answer gets feedback that explains why, so that mistakes also teach.

      The activities follow the progression of urban and environmental literacy: recognizing the mosquito and breeding sites, understanding the relationships between water, climate, waste and health, deciding and taking part. The central question runs through the whole issue: at the end of each theme, the child gets a clue to the answer, and the clues come together in the last theme. The activities that take the investigation off the screen (the home checklist, the school investigation and the weekly mission) are always done with an adult, without climbing to high places. The health information follows the Ministry of Health's guidelines, without recommending medicines, and the simulations use illustrative values, identified on screen.

      The language is simple, the drawings are stylized, and there are accessibility features: audio of the speech and instructions, and translation into Libras (Brazilian Sign Language) via the VLibras Suite in the Portuguese version. Progress is tracked with stars and ends with the weekly mission and the diploma. The issue is aligned with the BNCC skills (BRASIL, 2018) and the 2030 Agenda targets (NAÇÕES UNIDAS, 2015), listed in the panels below.

      Rationale for the activities

      Portrait of the mosquito, Find the mosquito!, Does every mosquito transmit dengue? and Dengue, Zika and chikungunya
      They build the basic repertoire to “read” the problem. The child explores the parts of the mosquito with a magnifying glass, applies this knowledge to tell Aedes aegypti apart from other insects, understands that only the female carrying the virus transmits the disease and that any female can start to transmit it, and tells the three diseases apart, which have the same vector and the same prevention (BRASIL, [2026a]; [2026b]; [2026c]).
      The mosquito's life cycle, Where does the mosquito lay its eggs?, It rained in the backyard! and Rain + heat + standing water
      They explain why standing water is the core of prevention. The child puts the stages of the cycle in order and tests, on the calendar, that emptying and scrubbing the container before the ninth day prevents the mosquito from being born (FIOCRUZ, [20--]a); investigates with a magnifying glass where the female lays her eggs and finds out, in the “bucket lab”, that they stick above the waterline and survive dry conditions until the water rises (FIOCRUZ, [20--]b); predicts which backyard objects will collect water, checks after the rain and fixes each breeding site, realizing that even a bottle cap collects water; and, in the simulator, relates the season and collective care to the number of mosquitoes, with illustrative values.
      Breeding site hunt!, 10 minutes against dengue, Is my home protected?, Dengue detectives and Before and after
      They turn knowledge into action at home. The child chooses the right action for each breeding site on the roof terrace (cover, turn over, add sand, store, wash, unclog, screen); plans an efficient ten-minute check of a house shown in cross-section, deciding the route and what to check in each room (LARA NETO, 2016); applies a real checklist with the family; searches, with a flashlight and against the clock, for hidden breeding sites in a backyard at night, separating them from what poses no risk; and compares two scenes of the same recreation area, one week apart, to identify what got better, what got worse and how to fix it, understanding that prevention is a routine, not a one-time action.
      Shall we count the breeding sites? and Maze against dengue
      They connect the topic to Mathematics: counting with the help of marks on the scene itself, addition, subtraction and multiplication in checking situations, reading a bar chart and spatial orientation in the maze.
      What about the school, is it protected?, Dengue is also a city problem and Waste in the wrong place can become a breeding site
      They widen the scale from the house to the school and the city. The class investigates five school areas (schoolyard, garden and vegetable garden, sports court, bathrooms, storeroom and cafeteria), decides what the school should do about each problem and produces a report for the principal; relates seven problems on a street to the public services that solve them, including basic sanitation services, which cover water supply, sewage, urban cleaning and drainage (BRASIL, 2007), and points out, for each one, what residents can do; and disposes of solid waste correctly, following the shared responsibility set out in the National Solid Waste Policy (Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) (BRASIL, 2010).
      How does the mosquito transmit dengue?, What are the symptoms of dengue?, Taking care of dengue the right way and Myths and facts
      They deal with health in language suited to children and without recommending medicines. The child puts together the transmission sequence, learns the symptoms and warning signs, follows, in six illustrated scenes, the story of a sick child and chooses care actions (tell an adult, go to the health center, drink fluids, rest and not self-medicate), and checks false information against information from health sources, in illustrated myth-or-fact cards (BRASIL, [2026a]; 2024).
      The endemic disease control agent and Everyone does their part
      They introduce the endemic disease control agent, the professional responsible for disease surveillance, prevention and control (BRASIL, 2006): the child puts together the agent's work kit, separating the tools from what isn't part of the visit, and follows a home visit in four scenes, including safety guidance for welcoming the professional; and they divide responsibilities among family, school, community and government.
      Fill in the words, Word search, Memory game and Weekly mission against dengue
      They review the issue's vocabulary and actions (in Fill in the words, in three stages: completing the words from clues, finding the secret word and fitting each word into a sentence) and bring prevention into the weekly routine, with a sheet for the child to check the different areas together with an adult.
      SDGs and the 2030 Agenda

      The 2030 Agenda brings together 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 169 targets, adopted by the 193 Member States of the United Nations in 2015 (NAÇÕES UNIDAS, 2015). SDG 3 is the central theme of this issue, and five other goals connect with it.

      In Brazil, surveillance, prevention and control of mosquito-borne diseases are part of the Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS) and rely on the work of endemic disease control agents (BRASIL, 2006). Basic sanitation (BRASIL, 2007) and solid waste management (BRASIL, 2010) are also essential to reduce breeding sites.

      • 3Good health and well-being

        SDG 3Good health and well-being

        • Target 3.3By 2030, end the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and neglected tropical diseases and combat hepatitis, water-borne diseases and other communicable diseases.
        • Target 3.8Achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all.
        • Target 3.dStrengthen the capacity of all countries, in particular developing countries, for early warning, risk reduction and management of national and global health risks.

      BNCC

      Skills from Brazil's National Common Core Curriculum (Base Nacional Comum Curricular, BNCC) (BRASIL, 2018) that this issue's activities help develop, from 1st to 5th grade, with some 7th-grade skills for older classes. Each skill comes with the official text and the activities where it is practiced. Tap a code to see the skill highlighted.

      • EF02CI04Science, 2nd grade: Describe characteristics of plants and animals (size, shape, color, life stage, place where they grow, etc.) that are part of their daily lives and relate them to the environment in which they live.
